question: How many confirmed 2026 US measles cases will the CDC report in its weekly update closest to October 1, 2026?

calls.reasoning: Resolves off the CDC headline in the Thursday Oct 1, 2026 update — exactly two weekly increments after the Sep 17 level of 3,471. Reference class: two-week changes in the CDC cumulative 2026 count during the current sustained-growth regime. The last three non-overlapping two-week sums were 312, 357 and 337, so the prior anchor is ~3,811. I adjust slightly up (~3,826) rather than down: the growth engines are new, not exhausted — Pennsylvania is adding 91-117/wk at the state level across 38 counties, Ohio jumped 47 in a week (327% over the prior week) with 29 suspected/probable still pending lab confirmation in Wayne County alone, and Wisconsin roughly doubled; the two large 2026 outbreaks that could decelerate the total (South Carolina, closed April 27; Utah, no new cases for 3+ weeks) are already contributing near zero, so their stall is priced into the observed run rate rather than a fresh drag. Counterargument for a lower number: the +211 week of Aug 20 shows increments are lumpy and mean-reverting, PA's Lancaster County core (324 cases) may be approaching saturation, and CDC-to-state reporting lag means a PA peak would show up in the national tally with a delay I cannot observe yet. Calendar risk is clear: Oct 1 is a Thursday exactly 14 days after Sep 17, and the FY2027 shutdown that could have disrupted publication was averted by a CR signed Sep 2 funding agencies through Dec 11. Tails: p_below_lower 1% — a cumulative YTD count only falls via a mass reclassification or methodology change (the CDC is already revising its measles DEATH definition, showing such changes happen); p_above_upper 1.5% — reaching 4,300 needs +829 in two weeks, ~2.4x the largest observed two-week sum, requiring an unprecedented retrospective batch addition. Market check: no contract matches this question's terms; Polymarket's $7.97M year-end market (same CDC source, Dec 31 deadline) implies a ~5,700-5,800 year-end median, i.e. ~150/wk sustained continuation, which corroborates the run-rate assumption without anchoring the two-week number. Kalshi returned HTTP 429.

calls.reconciliation: Three disputes mattered. (1) CDC's own Sep 17 figure for Pennsylvania: Run 3 reports 637 against PA DOH's 767, Runs 1 and 2 report 767. Unsettleable without retrieval on this run, but Runs 1 and 2 quote a CDC number identical to the state release - the signature of conflating the two sources - while Run 3's neighbouring values (SC 670, UT 526) match Run 1's independently-reported SC/UT figures. I lean toward the gap being real but refuse to bank it as Run 3 does: CDC trailing state dashboards is a standing property of the instrument, already embedded in the observed 160-211/wk run rate, not an extra bolus on top of it. It survives as a small rightward tilt, which is why my median sits at 3,825 rather than Run 3's implied 3,821-via-+350 or the bare anchor of 3,806. (2) The Aug 27 headline value is unrecoverable in all three dossiers; it is irrelevant, since the anchor uses non-overlapping two-week sums that skip it. (3) Publication continuity and the absence of a matching market were unanimous across runs and internally consistent (Thursday date, CR signed Sep 2 through Dec 11, no holiday); settled by agreement. The remaining split - accelerating (Runs 1, 3) vs decelerating (Run 2) - is pure judgment that the evidence does not break: the weekly series is flat while geographic breadth grows. I take continuation, the reading I would bet on. Where I depart from all three runs is dispersion: their 215-275 over-trusts a three-observation sample of two-week sums. Full-series weekly SD (~55) scaled to a two-week horizon and widened for a series that quadrupled its run rate inside six weeks supports ~265, so my interval is wider than any member's while the central estimate sits within their range.
